description:
Black Kraft Boxes, Dyed Rather Than Printed

There are two ways to get a black kraft box and they are not the same product. Dyeing the pulp before the sheet is made gives board that is black all the way through, so a cut edge and the inside of the box are black too. Printing black over brown kraft covers the outside only, and every crease and cut edge shows brown. At Kraft Box Pack we supply Black Kraft Boxes both ways and the choice matters more than most buyers expect.

Whether you are sourcing black kraft boxes wholesale or matching an existing range, the deciding question is whether the box is ever seen open.

Why dyed board wins on an open box

Edges and interiors

A lid lifted on a printed-black box reveals brown, which reads as a black box that has been cheaply made rather than as a deliberate contrast. Dyed board is black inside and out, and on any format opened in front of the customer — lidded, drawer, magnetic — that is the whole difference.

Ink coverage on brown

Covering brown with black takes a heavy ink lay, and heavy coverage on uncoated board can look patchy and mark easily. Dyed stock has no coverage problem because there is nothing to cover.

Where printed black is the right answer

On a tuck end opened once and discarded, or where black is a panel rather than the whole box, printing is cheaper and nobody sees an edge. It is also the only option when the design needs black in some places and kraft brown in others.

What black does to everything printed on it

Black board is the hardest ground to print on. Ordinary inks disappear into it, so colour on black needs either a white underbase printed first or a finish that sits on the surface rather than soaking in. Foil, spot UV and emboss all work particularly well for that reason, which is why black packaging so often uses them — it is a practical constraint that happens to look expensive.

Key elements of black kraft box design

  1. Dyed board wherever the box is opened in front of the customer.

  2. Printed black only where edges are never seen.

  3. Foil, spot UV or emboss rather than ink for detail.

  4. A white underbase where colour has to appear.

  5. Matte finish, which hides handling marks better than gloss.

Comparison with Brown Kraft Boxes

The two carry opposite signals from the same material. Brown Kraft Boxes read as natural, honest and unbleached; black reads as formal and premium. Ranges often use both deliberately — brown for the everyday line, black for the premium one — and because the structure is identical, they can share a dieline and differ only in the board.

Marks, and the practical downside

Black shows everything. Fingerprints, scuffs and dust are all visible on a dark matte surface in a way they are not on brown, which is why black packaging looks superb in a photograph and needs more care in a warehouse. A matte laminate resists it best; gloss shows the most.

Use Board Detail Finish Notes
Premium lidded and rigid Dyed through Foil or emboss Matte Interior is black too
Drawer and magnetic Dyed through Foil Matte Edges seen on opening
Retail tuck ends Printed black Spot UV Matte Cheaper, edges show brown
Mixed brown and black design Printed black Any Any Only printing allows both
Colour on black Either White underbase Any Extra pass required
High-handling ranges Dyed through Emboss Matte laminate Hides marks best

Eco Friendly Black Kraft Packaging

Dyed board recycles in the paper stream like any other kraft, and the dye does not prevent it. A plastic laminate over black does, which is worth knowing when a matte laminate is being specified to resist marking — a water-based matte varnish achieves much of the same and keeps the pack recyclable. The wider Colored Kraft Boxes range holds the same structures in other through-dyed shades.

What to send with your enquiry

The format, whether the box is opened in front of the customer, and whether any colour has to print on the black. The first two decide dyed or printed; the third decides whether you need an underbase.

Matching black across a range

Black is harder to match than it looks. Dyed board and printed black rarely sit at exactly the same shade, and two dyed batches can differ slightly as well. Where a collection uses both methods across different formats, the difference shows when the boxes sit together on a shelf.

The usual answer is to keep one method across everything a customer sees at once, and accept a difference only where the formats are never displayed together. Where an exact match matters across a long-running range, ordering the board for the whole range in one batch removes most of the variation.

Choose Black Kraft Boxes from Kraft Box Pack, dyed where it shows and printed where it does not. We provide:

  • Free design and free shipping

  • Through-dyed and surface-printed black, quoted side by side

  • Food-safe and eco-friendly kraft material

  • Fast turnaround times at wholesale rates

Send the format and we will tell you whether dyed board is worth the difference.

description:
Brown Kraft Boxes, and Why Brown at All

Brown kraft is brown because nothing was done to it. Bleaching costs money, weakens the fibre and removes the lignin that gives the board its colour, so unbleached kraft is both cheaper and stronger than the white equivalent. At Kraft Box Pack we cut Brown Kraft Boxes across every format, and that combination — cheaper and stronger — is why the material is where it is.

Whether you are sourcing brown kraft boxes wholesale or specifying a first range, the thing to understand about brown is what it does to everything printed on it.

Natural Texture That Enhances Product Display

What the material signals

Unbleached board reads as unprocessed, which over the last decade has moved it from cheap to considered. That works for natural, artisan and food-led brands and works against ranges positioned as traditional luxury, where white or black still signals more.

Colour on a brown ground

Every ink laid on brown warms and darkens. Dark colours cope; pale ones do not, because there is not enough pigment to hide the board underneath, and a soft pastel can read as beige. A white underbase fixes it at one extra pass, or the palette is chosen knowing the ground is warm.

Where brown flatters

Warm tones, food photography, foil and emboss all read better on brown than on white. Foil in particular has more contrast against a dark ground, which is why so much premium kraft packaging uses it rather than colour.

Virgin, recycled and the visible difference

Virgin brown kraft is a lighter, more even shade with longer fibres and more strength. Recycled is darker, flecked and a little weaker at the same weight. Neither is better — the flecks read as authentically recycled to some buyers and as cheap to others, and it is worth deciding which your customer sees rather than letting a supplier choose.

Key elements of specifying brown kraft

  1. Virgin where strength or an even shade matters.

    Recycled where the flecked look is wanted.

  2. A white underbase where the palette is pale.

  3. Foil and emboss rather than ink for premium detail.

  4. One board across a range, since shade varies between batches.

  5. Finishes chosen to keep the recyclability the material offers.

Comparison with Kraft Boxes With Lid

Brown is a material choice; the closure is a separate one, and the two are often confused in a brief. Kraft Boxes With Lid covers the two-piece builds that suit gifting and reuse, and the same brown board makes a tuck end, a mailer or a drawer just as well. Deciding the material and the structure separately gives a clearer specification than treating them as one product.

Batch variation, and planning around it

Natural kraft shade drifts between production batches because the pulp does. On a single order nobody notices. On a range reordered over two years, two boxes side by side can differ visibly, and customers do notice that. Ordering the board for a whole range in one batch removes most of it.

Need Stock Detail Finish Notes
Even shade, strength Virgin kraft Any Uncoated Lighter, more consistent
Recycled positioning Recycled kraft Any Uncoated Darker and flecked
Pale brand palette Either White underbase Any Extra print pass
Premium without colour Virgin kraft Foil or emboss Uncoated Contrast beats print here
Fine print detail White-top kraft Full colour Coated White face, brown back
Recyclable programmes Recycled kraft Any Water-based varnish No laminate or film

Custom Printing and Design Options for Kraft Boxes

Where a range needs colour as well as brown, the Colored Kraft Boxes collection holds the same structures in through-dyed board, so a coloured box and a brown one from the same range match in build and differ only in stock.

What to send with your enquiry

Your brand colours, whether the range will be reordered over years, and what the box has to protect. The first decides whether you need an underbase, the second whether to buy board in one batch, the third the structure.

Where brown costs you nothing and where it costs you a pass

On dark and warm palettes, brown is free — the colours sit on it well and the material does work that print would otherwise have to. On pale, cool or precisely matched palettes it costs a white underbase, which is a print pass across the whole box and a real line on the quote.

The choice worth making early is whether the brand adapts to the material or the material is made to carry the brand. Both are legitimate; only one of them is cheap, and deciding late means paying for artwork twice.

Finishes, and what they cost in recyclability

Plain brown kraft goes into the paper stream with nothing to separate. A gloss laminate, a film window or a foil block each break that for the part they cover. A water-based matte varnish gives much of the protection a laminate does and keeps the pack recyclable, which is usually the better trade where a claim is being made on the box.

  • Gloss, matte, and spot UV coating options

  • Free design and free shipping

  • Virgin, recycled and white-top brown stocks

  • Food-safe and eco-friendly kraft material

  • Fast turnaround times at wholesale rates

Send your brand colours and we will tell you whether they need an underbase.

description:
Colored Kraft Paper Wholesale for Packaging and Craft Use

Kraft is brown because it is unbleached, and that matters for colour: every pigment laid on it sits over a warm brown ground rather than a white one. Dyeing the pulp before the sheet is made gives a deep, through-coloured paper; printing a colour onto brown kraft gives a duller, warmer version of the same shade. Both are sold as coloured kraft and they are not the same product.

At kraft box pack we supply colored kraft paper both ways. Whether you are sourcing colored kraft paper wholesale in sheets or on the roll, the first question is whether the colour needs to go all the way through the fibre or only across the face.

Dyed through, or printed on

Dyed in the pulp

The colour is in the fibre, so a torn or cut edge shows the same shade as the face. That is what makes dyed stock right for anything folded, die-cut or torn on purpose — wrapping, tags, shredded fill — because there is no white or brown core to give it away.

Printed on the surface

A flood of ink across brown kraft is cheaper for short runs and lets you match a brand colour more exactly, but the cut edge stays brown and heavy folding can crack the ink along the crease. It suits flat uses — sheets, sleeves, printed wraps — better than heavily folded ones.

GSM, and what it is actually telling you

GSM is weight per square metre, not thickness, and it is the closest thing to a single number for how a paper behaves. Below about 80 gsm the sheet is for wrapping and void fill. Between 80 and 120 it takes folding, which is tissue and gift wrap territory. From 120 to 200 it holds a crease and works for tags, sleeves and bags. Above 200 it is board rather than paper and starts to behave like a carton stock.

Two sheets at the same GSM can still feel different depending on how they were made — a bulkier sheet feels substantial at a lower weight. Where the feel matters, a sample tells you in seconds what a number cannot.

Colour matching on a brown ground

A colour approved on a white proof will not look the same on kraft. Light colours are the worst affected, because there is not enough pigment to hide the ground beneath — a pale blue on brown reads grey-green. Where a brand colour has to be exact, either a white underbase is printed first, which costs an extra pass, or the colour is chosen knowing it will warm up.

Key elements of specifying coloured kraft

  1. Dyed through or surface printed, decided by whether edges show.

  2. GSM chosen for the use, from wrapping to tag stock.

  3. A white underbase where a brand colour has to be exact.

  4. Sheets or roll, decided by how it will be cut.

  5. Recyclability checked, since some dyes and coatings affect it.

Where colour is the whole product

On packaging, coloured kraft does something printing cannot — it colours the inside of the box as well as the outside, with no extra pass. For anyone specifying an interior colour, dyed stock is usually cheaper than printing the inner face. That is the reasoning behind Black Kraft Boxes, where the through-colour is the point rather than a finish over brown.

Color-Coded Sheets for Organized Presentation

Coloured stock is often bought to code a range — a shade per product line, per size or per season — which makes picking faster in a stockroom and reads as deliberate on a shelf. Where that colour needs to carry across boxes as well as paper, the Colored Kraft Boxes range holds the same shades in carton form so the two match.

faqs.question: What is colored kraft paper used for
faqs.answer: Colored kraft paper is used for gift wrapping, school crafts, packaging, and retail displays. It provides a strong and attractive texture while staying eco-friendly. Many businesses also use it for printed branding sheets and event decorations.

faqs.question: Is colored kraft paper safe for wrapping food
faqs.answer: Yes, when ordered with a protective coating or food-grade lining, kraft paper becomes safe for wrapping bakery and deli items. It prevents oil stains and maintains hygiene. Many bakeries prefer kraft because it reduces plastic usage.

faqs.question: Can I get colored kraft paper in roll and sheet form
faqs.answer: Yes, colored kraft paper rolls are supplied for bulk wrapping, while sheets are used for printing and gift packaging. Both options can be cut to custom sizes. Businesses select formats based on their daily usage and storage needs.

faqs.question: Does the color fade over time
faqs.answer: The dyes used in colored kraft paper are processed to resist fading during storage and handling. Proper indoor storage keeps colors fresh for months. Darker shades stay more stable under sunlight compared to light pastel tones.

faqs.question: Can kraft paper be printed with logos
faqs.answer: Yes, kraft paper sheets for printing support CMYK and PMS inks. Digital, offset, and screen printing all work smoothly on the surface. Retailers add barcodes, taglines, and branding artwork to improve customer experience.

faqs.question: What GSM thickness is available
faqs.answer: Colored kraft paper comes in multiple GSM options including 60–80 GSM for crafts, 90–120 GSM for packaging, and 140–200 GSM for heavy-duty wrapping. GSM selection depends on product weight and purpose. Higher GSM provides more strength.

faqs.question: Is colored kraft paper eco-friendly
faqs.answer: Yes, kraft paper is recyclable and biodegradable. It can be produced using FSC-certified materials to support sustainable sourcing. Many businesses prefer kraft paper as an eco-safe alternative to plastic and foil wrapping.

faqs.question: Can colored kraft paper be laminated
faqs.answer: Yes, gloss, matte, and Spot UV laminations can be applied for added shine or surface protection. Lamination helps protect the sheet while giving a polished appearance. It is commonly used for gift packaging and branded wraps.

faqs.question: Do you offer bulk pricing
faqs.answer: Bulk and wholesale orders come with discounted rates. The cost per sheet decreases as the order size increases. Large orders also include free design assistance and priority shipping options.

faqs.question: Which colors are available
faqs.answer: Colored kraft paper is available in red, blue, black, yellow, green, pink, and more. Custom color runs are also possible through special dye processing. Seasonal shades are supplied for holidays and event themes.

faqs.question: Can kraft paper be used for school projects
faqs.answer: Yes, it is widely used in classrooms for chart work, crafts, and display boards. The surface is smooth enough for coloring and drawing. Teachers prefer kraft sheets because they are durable and easy to cut.

faqs.question: Is kraft paper strong enough for shipping wrap

description:
Custom Kraft Bags, Held Up by the Handle

A bag has one structural problem and it is always the same: everything the bag carries hangs from where the handle meets the paper. At Kraft Box Pack we specify Custom Kraft Bags from the loaded weight and the handle attachment, because that joint is where bags fail and it fails in a customer's hand.

Whether you are sourcing kraft bags wholesale for retail or takeaway, the decisions are the handle type, the paper weight and whether the base is reinforced.

Handles, and what each will carry

Twisted paper

Glued to a reinforced patch inside the bag, comfortable to hold and the strongest of the paper options. It is the default for retail because it carries real weight without cutting into a hand.

Flat paper tape

Cheaper, thinner and fine for light loads. Under weight it cuts into the fingers, which customers notice more than they notice the bag.

Die-cut

A hole punched in the top of the bag with no separate handle at all. It costs nothing, keeps the bag entirely paper for recycling, and it tears first — so it belongs on light items.

Rope and ribbon

Knotted through eyelets, the premium option. Strong, comfortable and the only handle that reads as luxury, at a cost per bag several times the alternatives.

The base is the other failure

A flat-bottom bag with a reinforced card insert stands up on a counter and carries weight without the base bowing out. Without that insert the base rounds under load and the contents shift, which is how a bag that seemed fine in the shop splits on the walk home.

Key elements of kraft bag design

  1. Handle chosen for the heaviest realistic load.

  2. A reinforced patch where the handle attaches.

  3. Card base insert on anything with weight.

  4. Paper weight matched to the load, not to the print.

  5. Gusset sized so the bag stands open for filling.

Comparison with Kraft Dispenser Boxes

Both are formats where the structure has to survive being used rather than just shipped. Kraft Dispenser Boxes lose part of a panel and must still stand; a bag is loaded and lifted repeatedly. In both cases the specification is about the moment of use rather than the moment of packing, which is unusual in packaging.

Print, and the surface you actually see

A bag is seen folded flat on a counter and swinging from a hand, so the front panel and the lower half do the work — the top few centimetres disappear into the fold and the grip. Designs centred vertically often end up half-hidden in use.

Uncoated kraft absorbs ink and softens fine detail, which suits bold marks and works against small type. Most of the strongest retail bags carry one colour and a clear shape for that reason rather than for economy.

Bags within a packaging range

Bags usually carry boxes, and the Kraft Packaging Boxes range covers the cartons that go inside them. Matching the print across both is what makes a purchase look like it came from one brand rather than a shop that buys bags separately.

What to send with your enquiry

The heaviest thing the bag will carry, whether it needs to stand open on a counter, and whether the contents are greasy. The first sets the handle and paper, the second the gusset and base, the third the treatment.

Sizes, and the two that most shops actually need

Retailers tend to accumulate bag sizes and use two of them. A medium that fits most purchases and a large for the occasional bulky one covers the majority of transactions, and holding fewer sizes means larger runs, better prices and less storage.

Where a shop genuinely needs a third, it is usually a small bag for single items — and that is often better served by a paper wrap or a sleeve than by another bag, since a small purchase in a bag it barely fills looks worse than no bag at all.

Recyclability, and what breaks it

An all-paper bag with paper handles goes into the paper stream with nothing to separate. A rope handle, a plastic-coated finish or a laminated surface each end that. Where a bag carries a recycling claim, the handle choice usually decides whether it is true, and it is the part most often overlooked.

Storage before use

Bags arrive flat and take little room, which is one of their practical advantages over boxes. Where a shop orders a year's worth to get a better price, that is genuinely storable in a way the same value of cartons would not be.

description:
Kraft Art Supply Packaging, Where a Long Box Is a Beam

Art materials are longer than they are anything else. Brushes, pencils, charcoal and pastels all want a narrow box two or three times its own width, and a box in that proportion behaves like a beam — it sags in the middle when it is picked up by one end. At Kraft Box Pack we specify Kraft Art Supply Packaging around that flex, because the contents are exactly the things that snap.

Charcoal and soft pastels break if the box they are in bends by a few millimetres, and the box will bend unless something stops it.

Two problems in the same box

Long items flex

A long narrow carton needs either a heavier caliper than its weight suggests or an internal tray running its length. The tray is usually cheaper and it also seats the items, so it solves both problems at once.

Mixed sets are wildly uneven

A starter set might hold a jar of medium, a pad of paper and a handful of pastels. The jar weighs more than everything else combined and it will find the pastels on the first journey. Anything dense has to be compartmented away from anything brittle, whatever the layout looks like on a screen.

Pigment marks everything

Soft pastel and charcoal shed constantly. Left loose they coat the inside of the pack and the paper next to them, so a set that arrives looking used is not damaged, only badly divided.

Key elements of art supply pack design

  1. A full-length tray, since long boxes flex and brittle media snap.

  2. Heavy items compartmented away from fragile ones.

  3. Pigment-shedding media seated and separated from paper.

  4. A closure that survives being reopened for months.

  5. A front that shows the set, since these sell on contents.

The pack becomes the storage

Art materials are used over months and go back into their box every time, which is unusual for a retail carton and changes what wears out. The closure sees hundreds of cycles, the tray gets emptied and refilled, and the whole thing lives on a shelf or in a bag rather than being discarded. A hinged lid or a firm friction fit lasts; a tuck flap on light board is torn within a term of school use.

Selling a set the buyer cannot open

Nobody buys art materials without knowing exactly what is in the set, and the count, sizes and colours are the whole proposition. That pushes towards a window or a clearly printed contents panel, and the contents panel has to be specific — twelve pencils in a stated grade range sells, "assorted drawing pencils" does not. On a gift purchase, where the buyer is not the artist, that specificity is doing most of the work.

Comparison with Kraft Pencil Packaging Boxes

The two overlap and separate on breadth. Kraft Pencil Packaging Boxes hold one item type at one length, so the tray is a repeated slot and the whole pack can be tuned to a single dimension. An art supply pack holds several unrelated items of different weights and fragilities, so the interior has to be designed compartment by compartment.

Kraft in a category built on colour

Art packaging is usually a riot of swatches, and brown board against that reads as professional restraint. It suits materials sold on quality rather than on brightness, and it takes foil and single-colour printing very well. What it does badly is colour accuracy — a printed swatch on a brown base is not the colour in the tube, and where shade matching matters the pack needs either a window, a printed white base under the swatches, or real samples shown another way.

Shipping a long box

Long narrow parcels are handled badly by carriers and are the shape most likely to arrive with a bent corner. Where these are sold online, the outer needs to be stiff along its length rather than merely padded, and it is worth accepting a slightly larger outer to gain that rigidity. A crushed end on a brush set damages every item in it at once.

Materials rarely sell as a single line, and the Kraft Art Boxes collection covers the other formats a range needs. Sharing one board and one print treatment is what lets a shelf of very different shapes read as one brand.

The full contents list with the length of the longest item and the weight of the heaviest. Those two decide the tray and the compartments respectively.

description:
Kraft Bakery Bags for Bakers and Food Sellers

A bakery bag is the cheapest packaging in the shop and the one handled most, and it fails in a way boxes do not: it goes translucent. Butter and oil wick straight into paper, and a bag that looked clean at the counter is marked by the time the customer gets home. At Kraft Box Pack we specify Kraft Bakery Bags from the grease first, because everything else about them is easy.

Whether you are sourcing kraft bakery bags wholesale or comparing kraft bakery bags with window for a counter, the choice is between a greaseproof liner, a treated paper, or accepting the mark on items where it does not matter.

Why bakeries choose Kraft Bakery Bags

Grease, and the three ways to handle it

Greaseproof lined bags stop oil entirely and cost the most. Grease-resistant treated kraft slows it enough for a short carry and costs less. Plain kraft is fine for bread and dry bakes and wrong for anything fried or buttered. Most bakeries need two of the three rather than one for everything.

Breathing, which paper does and plastic does not

This is the reason bread is still sold in paper. A paper bag lets moisture out, so a crust stays crisp; a plastic one traps it and the crust softens within the hour. Any coating that improves grease resistance reduces breathability, which is the trade to be aware of when a lined bag is chosen for a crusty product.

Windows, and where they weaken the bag

A window sells the product and cuts the bag's strength along the panel it sits in. On a light pastry that is irrelevant; on a loaded bag of rolls it is where the tear starts. Keeping the window away from the base and the side gussets keeps most of the strength.

Sizes, gussets and how a bag actually gets used

A flat bag suits thin items and lies neatly on a counter. A gusseted bag opens into a square base and stands up, which matters when staff fill it one-handed while serving. For anything filled at speed, the gusset is worth more than it costs, because a bag that will not stay open costs a second on every sale.

Key elements of bakery bag design

  1. Grease handling chosen per product, not per shop.

  2. Plain paper on crusty items, so they breathe.

  3. Windows kept clear of the base and gussets.

  4. Gusseted where staff fill one-handed.

  5. Space left for a sticker or label seal.

Comparison with Kraft Food Boxes

A bag protects nothing structurally — it carries and it presents. Anything decorated, layered or crushable needs Kraft Food Boxes instead, and most counters run both: bags for bread, rolls and single pastries, boxes for cakes and anything with icing on it.

Branding on a bag

Bags print cheaply in one or two colours and badly in full colour, because uncoated kraft absorbs ink and softens fine detail. That suits the format — a bold single-colour mark reads well and survives being crumpled, which a photographic design does not.

Leaving a clear area for a label is worth designing in. Most bakeries seal bags with a sticker anyway, and a sticker landing on top of printed artwork looks accidental where a space left for it looks planned.

Easy storage and retail display

Bags take almost no storage, which is their other advantage over boxes, and the Kraft Packaging Boxes range covers the box formats a counter needs alongside them. Matching the print across bags and boxes is what makes a counter look like one brand.

What goes in each bag, whether it is fried or buttered, and whether staff fill one-handed. The first two set the paper, the third settles flat or gusseted.

Cost, and why bags rarely justify much of it

A bakery bag costs a small fraction of a box and is thrown away within the hour, so the sensible ceiling on what to spend is low. That argues for one or two colours, a plain paper wherever the product allows it, and putting the saved money into the boxes, which are kept and photographed.

Where bags do repay attention is volume. A shop going through several thousand a week saves meaningfully by matching paper grades to products rather than buying the safest grade for everything — greaseproof lined for the fried items only, plain kraft for the bread, treated in between.

description:
Custom Kraft Boxes for Bakery Goods

Baked goods are still changing when they go in the box. Bread and pastry give off steam for a long while after they leave the oven, and whatever the box does with that steam decides how the product arrives. At Kraft Box Pack we specify Kraft Bakery Boxes around that first, because a box that traps moisture ruins a crust no matter how well it is printed.

Whether you are sourcing kraft bakery boxes wholesale for a production bakery or comparing kraft bakery boxes with window for a counter, the choice that shapes everything is whether the product is crusty, creamy or dry.

Benefits of kraft bakery packaging

Venting for anything crusty

Bread, viennoiserie and anything with a baked crust needs air movement or it softens within an hour. A vented box or a simple die-cut hole keeps the crust; a sealed one guarantees it goes leathery. This is the single most common mistake in bakery packaging and it costs nothing to avoid.

Sealing for anything creamy

Cream, ganache and buttercream want the opposite — a closed box that keeps them from drying and from picking up other smells in a fridge. Here a tight lid is right, and a grease barrier stops butterfat marking the outside.

A base that carries a wet load

A filled cake is heavy and the weight sits on the base for the whole journey. A reinforced or full-overlap base carries it; a single glued seam softens where moisture reaches it and gives way exactly when the box is lifted by the sides.

Height is the measurement people get wrong

Bakery boxes are usually specified too shallow. Icing, cream and decoration need clearance, and a lid resting on the top of a cake ruins it before it leaves the counter. Measuring the tallest decorated example rather than the cake itself is what avoids that, and the extra height costs very little.

Key elements of kraft bakery box design

  1. Vented for crusty products, sealed for creamy ones.

  2. Height measured to the tallest decoration, not the cake.

  3. Reinforced base where the load is heavy or wet.

  4. Grease barrier on anything buttery.

  5. Windows where the counter sells on appearance.

Relation with Kraft Shipping Boxes

Bakeries that post cakes need a second box, not a stronger one. A bakery box holds the product still and manages moisture; it is not built to be thrown into a van. Kraft Shipping Boxes take the handling as an outer, with the bakery box inside, which is the only arrangement that reliably delivers decorated goods intact.

Design considerations for bakery packaging

Assembly speed matters more in a bakery than almost anywhere, because boxes are made up during service with flour on your hands. A box that folds in one motion is worth paying for; a fiddly one costs a few seconds on every order at the worst possible time.

On print, kraft warms every colour, and baked goods photograph warm anyway, so kraft usually flatters them. Where a brand colour has to be exact across a range, a white underbase holds it.

Exploring kraft packaging across food categories

Above about eight inches square a box becomes awkward to carry flat, and a customer will tilt it. A handle keeps it level, and on celebration cakes that is the difference between arriving as made and arriving leaning. description:
Kraft Beard Oil Boxes, Sized to the Dropper

A beard oil carton holds a small glass bottle with a dropper cap, and almost every failure in the format comes from the same thing: the bottle moving. Glass against board scuffs the print from the inside, and a dropper cap catching on a fold cracks. At Kraft Box Pack we specify Kraft Beard Oil Boxes from the bottle and its cap together.

Whether you are sourcing beard oil boxes wholesale or specifying a first run, the measurements needed are the bottle diameter, the height including the dropper, and the fill volume.

The cap is the measurement people forget

Height including the dropper

A 30ml bottle is one height; the same bottle with a dropper bulb is noticeably taller. A carton cut to the bottle alone will not close, and that is discovered on the packing bench with several thousand boxes already made.

The bottle must not move

A snug internal footprint stops rattling; where the diameter varies across a range, a board collar makes one carton fit several bottles. Loose glass in a printed carton scuffs the inside face over a long delivery and can crack the dropper against a fold.

Oil is the second enemy

Carrier oils creep. A drop on the inside of an uncoated carton spreads and shows through as a translucent mark within days, which looks like a leak whether or not there was one. A grease-resistant inner face costs little and prevents an appearance problem that is otherwise impossible to explain to a customer.

What the panels have to carry

Cosmetic packaging carries a lot of mandatory information — ingredients, volume, batch, period after opening, responsible person address — and on a carton this small it needs planning rather than fitting in afterwards. Blocking that area out before design begins avoids the redraw that follows when the final compliance copy arrives.

Key elements of beard oil box design

  1. Height measured with the dropper cap fitted.

  2. Snug footprint or a collar, so the glass cannot move.

  3. Grease-resistant inner face against oil creep.

  4. Panel space blocked out for mandatory cosmetic copy.

  5. One carton across a range where a collar can absorb the difference.

Comparison with Kraft Mascara Boxes

The formats are close relatives — both are slim cartons around a small glass or plastic vessel with a wand or dropper. Kraft Mascara Boxes face the same rattle and the same compliance panel, and a brand running both can usually share a board, a print system and even a carton depth, varying only the footprint.

Print on a small panel

Fine type and hairline rules vanish at this size, and uncoated kraft spreads ink slightly into the fibre, which costs a little more legibility. Setting type larger than the design suggests, and proofing at actual size rather than on screen, is what avoids an ingredients panel nobody can read.

Foil and emboss work well here because the whole surface is close to the eye, and they cost less than on a large format simply because there is less area to cover.

Beard oil within a grooming range

Grooming lines grow into balms, waxes, combs and washes, and the Kraft Cosmetic Boxes range covers the jar, tube and set formats those need. Specifying them on one board and one print system from the start means adding a product later is a size change rather than a rebrand.

What to send with your enquiry

The bottle with its cap fitted, or its dimensions including the dropper, and the mandatory copy you have to carry. The first sets the carton, the second sets the layout.

Quantities and how the price actually moves

Small cartons are dominated by setup rather than board, so the unit price falls steeply from a few hundred to a couple of thousand and then flattens. A brand ordering five hundred and one ordering five thousand are paying very different prices per box for the same product.

Digital printing removes the plate cost and suits the short end; offset costs more to set up and less per unit once volumes climb. The crossover depends on the number of colours, so both are worth quoting rather than assuming which applies.

Adding products to a line

A grooming range that starts with one oil usually adds a balm, a wash and a comb within a year. description:
Kraft Board Game Packaging Boxes, and the Lid That Sags

A game box is a wide, flat lid over a wide, flat base, which is the least rigid shape in packaging. Stack a dozen of them in a warehouse for six months and the lids bow, the corners round off, and a shelf of them looks tired before a single copy is sold. At Kraft Box Pack we specify Kraft Board Game Packaging Boxes around that unsupported span.

It is a slow failure rather than a dramatic one, which is exactly why it gets designed in without anybody noticing.

What holds a game box up

The folded board is structural

A game board folded to the internal footprint sits under the lid and braces it across the whole span. That is not a happy accident — it is why game boxes are proportioned the way they are, and a game without a folding board loses the stiffest component it would have had.

The tray carries the stack

A moulded or die-cut component tray transmits the weight of the boxes above straight down through the walls rather than through the lid. Without one, the lid takes the load and the contents rattle underneath.

Base walls do the real work

Compression in a warehouse runs down the corners and walls of the base. A base wall that is a millimetre short of the lid's inner face is doing nothing, and the lid takes everything instead.

Key elements of game box design

  1. An internal tray, so stacking load bypasses the lid.

  2. Base walls that meet the lid, since the gap decides who carries the stack.

  3. Caliper set from the loaded weight, which is high for the size.

  4. A lid fit that stays easy after a hundred openings.

  5. Shrink wrap or a seal, because retail copies get opened.

Games are heavy for their footprint

Cards, a folded board, punchboard, dice and any miniatures add up quickly, and a mid-size game routinely weighs more than a small appliance packed in a box the same size. The base is lifted by its edges every time somebody takes it off a shelf, so the caliper follows the loaded weight rather than the dimensions, and a box specified from its footprint alone will fail at the base corners first.

A box opened hundreds of times

Unlike almost all retail packaging, a game box stays in use for years and is opened every time the game is played. A lid that fits tightly out of the factory becomes tight and then damaged as the board takes up moisture and swells slightly, and a lid that is torn at the corner is the most common complaint about game packaging. Specifying a slightly easy fit is the right call, even though a snug lid feels better on the first opening.

Comparison with Kraft Puzzle Packaging Boxes

The two share a shelf and not much else. Kraft Puzzle Packaging Boxes hold loose pieces and a single sheet, so there is nothing inside contributing any stiffness and the box has to provide all of it. A game box gets substantial help from its own folded board and component tray, which is why a puzzle box of the same size usually needs a heavier caliper than a game does.

Shipping to backers rather than to shops

A game sent to a shop travels inside a case on a pallet and never sees a courier directly. A game sent to a backer or an online customer is handled alone, and the retail box is not built for that — corner damage on a collectible box is treated as damage to the product itself. A plain outer carton is the answer, and it is cheap next to the reprint cost of a damaged box.

Printing on kraft for a game

Games sell on their cover art, and a brown base changes every colour laid over it. For an illustrated cover that usually means a printed white base under the artwork, which should be priced in from the start. Where a game is deliberately understated — a wooden abstract, a small press title — uncoated kraft with one or two colours does something no glossy box can, and that is the case where the material is a genuine advantage rather than a constraint.

Publishers rarely have one product, and the Kraft Toy Packaging collection covers the formats around a boxed game. A consistent board and finish across a catalogue is what makes a publisher's shelf recognisable at a distance.

Kraft Bouquet Boxes, Shaped Around Stems

A bouquet is wide at the top, narrow at the bottom and wet at the base, and a box for one has to answer all three at once. At Kraft Box Pack we cut Kraft Bouquet Boxes tapered for that reason — stems gather in the base while blooms open above without being pressed against a wall.

Whether you are sourcing bouquet boxes wholesale for a florist or a delivery service, the decisions are the taper, the liner and how the box travels.

Why the taper does the work

Stems gather, blooms open

A straight-sided box either crushes the blooms to fit the stems or wastes space around the stems to fit the blooms. A taper solves both, and it is the reason the shape exists rather than a decorative choice.

Height to the tallest bloom

Measured to the arrangement rather than the stems, with clearance above, because a lid or a wrap resting on the flowers marks them within hours. This is the same mistake made with cake boxes and it is equally avoidable.

The base holds water

Most bouquets travel with a water source or wet wrapping at the base, and board loses strength as it absorbs. A lined base keeps the water off, and a full-overlap construction carries the weight while it is doing so.

Standing or lying, which changes everything

A bouquet carried by hand travels upright and needs a wide, stable base. One posted travels lying down and needs the blooms held clear of the walls and the water source sealed so it does not empty into the box. These are two different builds, and florists doing both generally need both.

Key elements of bouquet box design

  1. Tapered, so stems gather and blooms open.

  2. Height measured to the tallest bloom, with clearance.

  3. Lined base, since water reaches the board otherwise.

  4. Wide base for carrying, sealed source for posting.

  5. A handle or ribbon, because a wet box is awkward to grip.

Comparison with Kraft Flower Boxes

The two overlap and are specified differently. Kraft Flower Boxes covers the hat-box and arranged formats where flowers sit in foam at a fixed height and the box is a container. A bouquet box holds a tied arrangement that has its own shape, so the box follows the flowers rather than the other way round.

Print, and what damp does to it

Condensation and water lift some inks and coatings, and a box that looked perfect in the shop can be marked by the time it is handed over. A water-based varnish or matte laminate resists that; uncoated print on the outside of a wet-lined box will eventually show it.

Foil holds up well on kraft and does not care about damp, which is why so much floral packaging uses a single foil mark rather than colour across the panel.

Kraft Box with Window for Retail Display

A window earns its place when the product sells itself and costs you when it does not. At Kraft Box Pack we cut Kraft Boxes with Windows knowing the trade behind them — every aperture removes stiffness from the panel it sits in, so the board usually steps up a grade to compensate, and that changes the quote rather than just the artwork.

Whether you are comparing kraft boxes with window wholesale or sizing an aperture for a range, the decision worth making first is filmed or open, because it decides both the protection and whether the pack stays recyclable.

Practical uses of kraft boxes with windows

Where to put the aperture

Keep it away from corners and creases. A window that runs close to a fold takes the strength out of exactly the part of the box doing the work, and the panel bows in a stack. Set back from the edges, the same aperture costs far less stiffness.

Filmed or open

Film keeps dust and hands off the product and lets you show food safely. An open die-cut keeps the pack in the paper stream without separation, which matters if recyclability is a claim you make. PET and PLA films behave differently at the recycling end, and that is a decision to make deliberately.

What the window should frame

A window showing an unremarkable part of the product is worse than no window, because it draws the eye to the wrong place. The aperture shape should be drawn around the thing worth seeing rather than centred out of habit.

Key elements of window box design

  1. Aperture set back from corners and creases.

  2. Board stepped up a grade to replace lost stiffness.

  3. Filmed for protection, open for recyclability.

  4. Shape drawn around the part worth showing.

  5. Flat-packed, with film applied before folding.

Comparison with Kraft Gift Boxes With Lids

A window sells to a stranger on a shelf; a lid sells to someone who has already bought. Ranges often need both, which is why window boxes pair with Kraft Gift Boxes With Lids — the window for retail display and the lidded build for gifting and direct orders, on one board and one print system.

Design considerations for retail shelves

Windows change how print is judged. The eye compares the product's real colour against the printed panel beside it, so a photograph on the pack that does not match what shows through the aperture reads as a mistake even when both are accurate.

Where the pack is filled by hand, a filmed window adds a step and a way to scratch the film. Testing a small run before committing usually finds that in an afternoon.

What a window costs, in board and in money

An aperture removes material from a panel that was carrying load, so the panel bends more easily and the box compresses sooner in a stack. A complex aperture costs more to cut, weakens the panel more than a simple one of the same area, and dates faster than a plain rectangle or circle. description:
Kraft Boxes For Gifts, Chosen by the Moment

Gift packaging is bought for a few seconds of experience, and almost every decision in it serves those seconds. At Kraft Box Pack we cut Kraft Boxes For Gifts starting from how the box should open, because the closure decides the feeling and everything else — board, insert, finish — follows from it.

Whether you are sourcing gift boxes wholesale for a retail range or a one-off run, the useful first question is not what size but what the opening should feel like.

What each closure says

Lid and base

Everything is revealed at once, and the empty box stays useful. This is the format people keep, which is why it suits anything sold as a keepsake or a set.

Drawer

A slow horizontal reveal with the recipient's hands on the box throughout. It costs more than a lid and cannot fall open in a bag, which suits ranges handled heavily in store.

Magnetic

A decisive click and a lid that opens flat, presenting a set laid out. The most expensive of the three and the most immediately impressive.

Tuck end

Cheapest, ships flattest, reads as retail rather than gift. The right answer when the box is a carrier and the wrapping happens afterwards.

The gap that ruins it

A gift box slightly too large for its contents reads as cheap whatever the board costs, because the gap is the first thing the eye finds. Either size to the product, or use an insert to close the space — a tray, a cushion or even tissue does it. This is the single most common failure in gift packaging and the cheapest to avoid.

Key elements of gift box design

  1. Closure chosen for how the opening should feel.

  2. Sized to the contents, or an insert to close the gap.

  3. Print inside the lid, which is what the eye lands on first.

  4. White underbase where the palette is pale on brown board.

  5. Rigid where the box is kept, folding where it is not.

Comparison with Kraft Paper Gift Wrapping

A box and a wrap solve the same problem at different price points. Kraft Paper Gift Wrapping adapts to any shape, costs a fraction and protects nothing; a box holds its form, stacks and survives a journey. Many ranges use both — the box for the product, the wrap for the seasonal layer over it.

What kraft does to a gift palette

Every colour on brown board warms and darkens, and pale shades suffer most because there is not enough pigment to cover the ground. A soft pastel can read as beige. Where a palette is light and fixed, a white underbase holds it at one extra pass; where it is dark or warm, kraft flatters it for free.

Foil and emboss are the usual way to add perceived value without colour, and both hold better on kraft than on white board because the brown gives them contrast.

Wraps, tags and the layer around the box

A gift range is rarely just boxes, and the Kraft Wrapping & Accessories collection covers the wraps, tags, ribbon and tissue that go with them. Specifying those from the same board family is what makes a set look designed rather than assembled from what was available.

What to send with your enquiry

Assembly, and who does the folding

Gift boxes are almost always delivered flat, and someone makes them up — usually your staff, at a counter, in the weeks when they have least time. A box that assembles in one motion rather than four is worth more in December than any saving on board, and that is a dieline decision made months earlier.

Where boxes are made up in advance, storage becomes the constraint instead, since an assembled box takes several times the space of a flat one. Ranges that sell in bursts usually settle on a quick-assembly build kept flat until the week it is needed.

Ribbon, tissue and the cost of a finish

Ribbon can be fitted in production or left for your team. Fitted, it costs more per unit and arrives finished; loose, it costs less and takes about twenty seconds a box. On a few hundred that is nothing; on several thousand it is a week of someone's time, and worth pricing both ways.

description:
Kraft Boxes With Lid, and the Gap Between Them

A two-piece box is two dielines, two print passes and two assembly steps, and all of that cost buys one thing: a lid that lifts off cleanly and goes back on. Whether it does is decided by a clearance of a few tenths of a millimetre. At Kraft Box Pack we set that clearance on Kraft Boxes With Lid for the conditions the boxes will actually live in.

Whether you are sourcing kraft boxes with lid wholesale or specifying a range, the questions are how often the box is opened and where it is stored.

Why the clearance is the product

Board moves with humidity

Paper takes up moisture from the air and swells slightly. A lid cut to fit perfectly in a dry factory binds in a damp warehouse, and one cut loose enough to be safe everywhere slides off in a bag. Neither is a manufacturing fault — it is a specification that has to know where the boxes are going.

Depth changes what it says

A shallow lid over a deep base reads as a presentation box. A deep lid covering most of the base reads as a shipper or a storage box. The same footprint reads as either, and it costs nothing to choose at dieline stage.

Rigid holds it, folding loosens

A folding lid is held square by creases, and creases relax with use. A rigid lid is held by a board core cut to shape and keeps its fit for years. Where the box is opened repeatedly, that difference is the whole reason to pay for rigid.

What a lid does that a tuck end cannot

It comes off completely, so the contents are revealed all at once and the empty box remains useful. That is why lidded boxes are kept and tuck ends are recycled, and why the format dominates gifting, keepsakes and anything sold as a set.

Key elements of lidded box design

  1. Clearance set for the storage humidity, not the factory.

  2. Lid depth chosen for how the box should read.

  3. Rigid where it is opened often, folding where it is not.

  4. Inside of the lid printed, since it is seen on opening.

  5. A ribbon pull on deep lids, so they lift without suction.

Comparison with Black Kraft Boxes

The structure and the material are separate decisions that briefs often merge. Black Kraft Boxes are about the board — dyed through so cut edges and interiors are black too — while the lid is about how the box opens. The same lidded build works in brown, black or any dyed stock, and deciding the two independently gives a much clearer specification.

Stacking, and the reason lids gap

Lidded boxes stack well, and a stack presses down on the lid of the box below. Where a lid is a fraction loose, that pressure racks it slightly out of square and it never sits quite right again. Specifying for the stack height as well as the contents is what prevents the range that looks fine on arrival and untidy after a month in a stockroom.

Choosing the board alongside the build

Once the structure is settled, the stock is a separate and equally consequential choice, and the Colored Kraft Boxes range holds the same lidded builds in through-dyed board. A collection can then vary colour across sizes while keeping one dieline family.

What to send with your enquiry

The contents, how often the box is opened, and where stock sits before it sells. The first sets the size and insert, the second decides rigid or folding, the third sets the clearance.

Assembly, and where the labour goes

Two pieces means two assembly steps, and on a folding build that is roughly double the time of a tuck end. At low volumes it is irrelevant; across several thousand it is a real cost, and pre-assembled bases are worth pricing against the labour they save.

Rigid boxes arrive assembled, which removes the labour and adds it to the freight instead, since they cannot be flat-packed. Which of the two costs more depends entirely on the distance and the quantity, and it is worth asking for both rather than assuming rigid is simply the expensive option.

Ribbon pulls and deep lids

A deep lid on a snug base can hold by suction, and a customer pulling harder is how a lid tears. A ribbon pull or a small die-cut vent breaks the seal and makes the lift smooth. It is a detail that costs almost nothing and is only noticed when it is missing.

Coatings reduce smudges by adding a protective layer between the kraft surface and routine handling. Matte coatings help lower glare and can hide small marks better under normal lighting. description:
Kraft Bulk Shipping Crates, Which Fail Slowly

Heavy-duty board does not usually give way to a single event. It gives way to a load held for weeks — a crate at the bottom of a stack loses strength gradually, and one morning the pallet is out of square. At Kraft Box Pack we specify Kraft Bulk Shipping Crates against sustained compression rather than against a drop test.

Which is a different number from the one most specifications quote, and it is the number that decides whether a warehouse stack is safe in a month's time.

What actually reduces a crate's strength

Time under load

Board creeps. A crate that comfortably holds a stated weight when it is loaded will hold noticeably less after several weeks of carrying it, and long-term storage has to be specified with that allowance built in.

Humidity

Corrugated board loses a large part of its compression strength in a damp environment, and an unheated warehouse in winter is a damp environment. This is the single biggest variable in real-world performance and it never appears in a catalogue figure.

Overhang on the pallet

A crate whose corners hang past the pallet edge has lost the support under the exact points that carry the stack. Even a small overhang cuts stacking strength substantially, which makes pallet fit a structural decision rather than a logistics one.

Key elements of crate specification

  1. Compression rated for the storage period, not the journey.

  2. A footprint that fits the pallet with no overhang.

  3. Board grade chosen for the storage humidity.

  4. Corners protected, since they carry the whole stack.

  5. Hand holds where crates are moved without equipment.

Corners carry everything

In a stacked pallet the load runs down the vertical corners, not through the panels. That is why a crate with crushed or rounded corners has lost most of its capacity even though its walls look intact, and why corner posts or reinforced verticals buy more strength per unit cost than a heavier board across the whole crate. When a stack fails, the corners are what to inspect.

Fitting the pallet, not the product

The temptation is to size a crate around the goods and take the pallet as it comes. Done that way, a pallet routinely carries less than it could and the crates overhang, which weakens the whole stack. Working the other way — dividing a standard pallet footprint into a whole number of crates and then fitting the product to that — usually produces a better crate, a fuller pallet and a lower cost per unit shipped.

Comparison with Kraft Industrial Parts Boxes

Both are working packaging rather than presentation, and they operate at different scales. Kraft Industrial Parts Boxes hold components at a workstation, are handled constantly by people, and are specified around lifting and picking. A bulk crate is handled by equipment, moved rarely and stacked for a long time, so its specification is dominated by static compression instead.

Crates that come back

Where crates run a closed circuit between two sites, they can be specified to fold flat and return, which changes the economics completely — a crate used twenty times can justify a much heavier board than one used once. It also introduces a requirement the single-use version never has: the crate must survive being knocked down and re-erected repeatedly, which is a different stress from carrying a load.

Marking a crate so it is handled properly

Weight, orientation, stacking limit and any handling restriction need to be printed large enough to read from a forklift, on more than one face. A crate marked on one side only will be turned, and everything printed on it becomes invisible at the moment it matters. This is cheap to get right and it is the most common gap on otherwise well-specified industrial packaging.

Within an industrial range

A site rarely needs crates alone, and the Kraft Industrial Packaging collection covers the transit and handling formats that go with them. One board specification across a site keeps stacking predictable, which is what makes a warehouse plan work.

What to send with your enquiry

The loaded weight, the stack height, how long crates sit loaded and the pallet you use. Storage time and humidity are the two that get left out and they change the answer most.

description:
Kraft Cake Boxes, Sized to the Decoration

A cake box has to hold something heavy, wet and fragile, and get it somewhere without touching it. That last part is what most cake packaging gets wrong: the lid rests on the icing and the cake is ruined before it leaves the counter. At Kraft Box Pack we specify Kraft Cake Boxes from the tallest decorated height rather than from the cake.

Whether you are sourcing kraft cake boxes wholesale for a bakery or comparing kraft cake boxes with window for a counter, the three numbers that matter are the cake diameter, the height to the top of the decoration, and the filled weight.

Why bakeries rely on Kraft Cake Boxes

Height, measured to the topper

Swirled buttercream, a drip finish, a topper or fresh flowers all add height that a size chart does not know about. Measure the tallest decorated example you sell and add clearance above it. This costs almost nothing at the dieline stage and is the single most common cause of remakes.

The base carries a wet load

A filled cake concentrates weight on the base, and moisture from the cake softens the board it sits on. A reinforced or full-overlap base carries that; a single glued seam gives way at the moment the box is lifted from underneath, which is always.

Moisture, and which direction

Cream and buttercream want a closed box that stops them drying and picking up fridge odours. Anything with a baked crust wants the opposite, or it goes leathery. Bakeries selling both usually need two builds rather than one compromise.

Handles, and where they become necessary

Above roughly eight inches square a box is awkward to carry flat, and a customer will tilt it. On a decorated cake, tilting is the failure. A die-cut handle keeps the box level and is cheap next to remaking a cake, so it is worth specifying from the size where tilting becomes likely rather than from the largest box you sell.

Key elements of cake box design

  1. Height to the tallest decoration, with clearance above it.

  2. Reinforced base, since the load is heavy and damp.

  3. Closed for cream, vented for crust.

  4. A handle from the size where a customer would tilt it.

  5. Grease barrier on anything buttery held overnight.

Comparison with Kraft Mailer Boxes

A cake box is not a shipper. Its job is to hold a cake still and manage moisture; a courier network will crush it and the decoration with it. Bakeries posting cakes use Kraft Mailer Boxes as an outer with the cake box inside, which is the only arrangement that reliably delivers a decorated cake intact.

Windows, and what they cost on a cake box

Cakes sell on appearance, so a window earns its place — and it removes stiffness from the lid, which is the panel already carrying the load in a stack. On larger sizes the board usually steps up a grade to compensate, which is a price change rather than an artwork one.

A window also shows condensation. On a cake boxed slightly warm, the film fogs and the customer sees a blurred cake, so venting matters more once a window is added rather than less.

Board loses strength as it takes up moisture, and a cake supplies moisture continuously. A box that felt rigid on the counter can be noticeably softer by the time it reaches a customer's kitchen, which is why cake boxes are specified a caliper heavier than the weight alone would suggest.

A grease-resistant liner slows the process as well as keeping butter off the outside, and on anything sold the following day it earns its cost twice. For same-day collection it is usually unnecessary.

Most decorated cakes sit on a board or drum inside the box, and that changes the internal dimensions. Specifying the box to the cake and then adding a half-inch drum is a common way to end up with a box that no longer closes, so the drum size belongs in the enquiry alongside the cake.

description:
Kraft Candle Boxes Wholesale Packaging

Candles are heavier than they look and they arrive as glass. A three-wick jar can run well over a kilogram, and all of that weight sits on the base of the box for the whole journey — which is why candle packaging fails at the base far more often than at the walls. At Kraft Box Pack we specify Kraft Candle Boxes from the weight and the vessel first.

Whether you are sourcing kraft candle boxes wholesale or comparing candle boxes with inserts for a gift range, the two numbers that decide the build are the filled weight and the diameter of the vessel at its widest point.

The base carries everything

Why a glued base is not enough

A single glued seam under a kilogram of glass will hold in the warehouse and give way when the parcel is dropped. A crash-lock or full-overlap base spreads the load across the whole underside, and on heavier candles that is the difference between a returned order and a delivered one.

The insert does the real work

Glass that moves inside a box breaks glass. A snug fitment — board collar, foam, or moulded pulp — stops the vessel travelling in the first place, and on a candle it matters more than the strength of the outer. The alternative is void fill, which costs labour on every unit and looks worse on opening.

Lids and the second use

Candle boxes are kept. A lid and base or a rigid build survives being opened and closed for as long as the candle burns, which is months, and a customer who keeps the box keeps the brand on a shelf.

Fragrance, and what it does to board

Scented wax is oily and volatile, and both matter to packaging. Fragrance oils migrate into uncoated board over months in storage, which dulls the print and can carry the scent to whatever sits next to it in a warehouse. Where candles are stored long or shipped in mixed loads, a barrier coating or a sealed vessel is the answer, and it is a decision worth making before a season's stock is made.

Key elements of candle box design

  1. Base construction rated for the filled weight, not the box size.

  2. A fitment sized to the vessel, so the glass cannot travel.

  3. Barrier where fragrance oils would otherwise reach the board.

  4. A closure that survives repeated opening, since the box is kept.

  5. Safety and burn instructions given panel space at layout stage.

Comparison with Kraft Jewelry Boxes

Both formats are built around protecting something fragile in a fitment, but the loads are opposite. Kraft Jewelry Boxes hold almost no weight and are specified for presentation; a candle box holds a kilogram and is specified for the drop. Using a jewellery build for a candle is the common and expensive mistake, because it looks right and fails in transit.

Design considerations for candle brands

Burn instructions and safety copy are required in most markets, and they need real space rather than the last gap left on the artwork. Blocking that area out before design starts avoids a redraw when the compliance text arrives.

On finish, matte reads warmer against wax and glass than gloss does, and it hides the handling marks a kept box will pick up. Foil on kraft holds well because the brown ground gives it contrast that white board does not.

description:
Kraft Candle Sleeve Boxes, the Cheapest Way to Brand a Candle

A sleeve is a band of printed board around a product that already holds its own shape. It uses roughly a third of the material of a carton and carries the same print, which makes it the most efficient branding there is — and it protects almost nothing, which is the trade. At Kraft Box Pack we cut Kraft Candle Sleeve Boxes for exactly the products that do not need protecting.

Whether you are sourcing candle sleeves wholesale or comparing a sleeve against a full carton, the deciding question is whether the vessel can survive being handled bare.

When a sleeve is the right answer

The vessel is the pack

A candle in a thick glass jar or a tin is already protected. Putting it in a carton adds cost, material and shipping volume to protect something that was not at risk. A sleeve puts the brand on it and leaves the vessel visible, which is often what the customer wanted to see anyway.

Fit is the whole specification

A sleeve too loose slides off in a bag; too tight and it will not go on without buckling, which shows immediately on a printed band. On tapered vessels the fit changes with height, so the sleeve position has to be fixed as well as its diameter.

Where it fails

Anything that can chip, scratch or break needs a carton. A sleeve gives no corner protection and no cushioning, and a candle posted in a sleeve alone arrives as glass in a padded envelope.

Fragrance, and what it does to board

Scented wax gives off oils that migrate into uncoated board over months in storage, dulling the print from behind. On a sealed vessel the sleeve is safe; on an open one, or where sleeves are stored loose alongside candles, a barrier coating or a sealed inner keeps the print looking as it was made.

Key elements of candle sleeve design

  1. Fit measured to the vessel at the exact height the sleeve sits.

  2. Sleeve only where the vessel protects itself.

  3. A barrier where fragrance oils could reach the board.

  4. Burn instructions and safety copy given panel space.

  5. A carton instead wherever the candle is posted.

Comparison with Kraft Beauty Kit Boxes

The two sit at opposite ends of the same decision. Kraft Beauty Kit Boxes exist to hold several items apart in a compartment tray, doing real structural work. A sleeve does none. Ranges commonly use both — sleeves for the single candles, a boxed set for the gift version — on one board and one print system.

Print on a band

A sleeve gives one continuous surface with a join, and where that join falls is an artwork decision. A repeating pattern hides it; a single mark placed badly runs straight through it. The usual approach is to put the brand on the front, the mandatory copy on the back, and the join at the side.

Sleeves also print well because they stay flat until they are applied, so registration is easier than on a folded carton and finishes like foil sit cleanly.

Applying sleeves, and the labour behind them

Sleeves are applied by hand in most small operations, and a well-fitted one takes a couple of seconds while a tight one takes several and occasionally buckles. Across a few thousand units that difference is real, and it is decided entirely by the tolerance set at dieline stage.

description:
Kraft Candy Boxes That Protect and Present

Confectionery is packaging's hardest food category, because sugar and chocolate fail in opposite conditions. Sugar draws moisture from the air and goes sticky; chocolate releases fat that migrates into board and blooms grey on the surface. At Kraft Box Pack we specify Kraft Candy Boxes from which of those two you are guarding against, since one box cannot do both well.

Whether you are sourcing kraft candy boxes wholesale for retail or building an event range, the first question is the product — hard sugar, soft sweets or chocolate — because each points at a different barrier.

Barriers, by what the sweet does

Sugar and moisture

Hard sweets, brittle and anything glazed pull moisture out of humid air and stick together. The barrier has to keep moisture out, which usually means a coated liner or a sealed inner bag inside the carton rather than treatment of the carton itself.

Chocolate and fat

Cocoa butter migrates into uncoated board over weeks, leaving a translucent stain and dulling the print from behind. A grease-resistant liner stops it. This is a storage problem more than a transit one, so it matters most on ranges that sit in a warehouse before a season.

Heat, which is nobody's friend

Chocolate blooms above roughly 22 degrees and never recovers its finish. Packaging cannot fix warehouse temperature, but a heavier board and a closed build slow the swing, and an insulated outer is worth specifying for summer shipping.

Counts, trays and the look of a full box

A candy box is judged on opening by whether it looks full. Loose sweets settle in transit and arrive looking short even when the weight is right, which is why a fitted tray with a cell per piece does more for perceived value than anything printed on the outside. Where a tray is not viable, filling to a count rather than to a volume is the next best thing.

Key elements of candy box design

  1. Barrier chosen for sugar or for chocolate, not for both.

  2. A tray or divider so the box reads full on opening.

  3. Food-contact grades on board, ink and coating alike.

  4. Ingredient and allergen panel given space at layout stage.

  5. Window options where the product sells on appearance.

Comparison with Kraft Gift Boxes With Lids

Much confectionery is bought as a gift, and there the build matters as much as the barrier. Kraft Gift Boxes With Lids covers the lidded formats that suit a boxed assortment, where the lift is part of the product. A retail candy carton and a gift assortment are two different specifications even when they hold the same sweets.

Design considerations for confectionery brands

Ingredient and allergen declarations are required and they take real space. Blocking that panel out before design begins avoids the redraw that follows when the final recipe copy arrives, which on a seasonal range is time you do not have.

Print on kraft warms every colour, and confectionery relies on appetite appeal more than most categories. A photograph of the sweets shot on white board will look duller on brown; either a white underbase or artwork designed for the warm ground solves it.

Product Main Risk Barrier Inner Notes

Bulk and Wholesale Kraft Candy Boxes

Confectionery ranges are seasonal and usually run several formats at once, and the Kraft Gift & Specialty Boxes collection covers the lidded, window and drawer builds those seasons tend to need. Ordering them on one board and one print system is what keeps a seasonal range looking planned.

What to send with your enquiry

The product, the count per box, and how long stock sits before it sells. The first two set the barrier and the tray; the third decides how much the storage risk matters.

Shelf life, and what packaging can actually do

Packaging does not extend shelf life so much as protect the life the product already has. A sealed inner bag inside a printed carton does the preserving; the carton does the presenting and the stacking. Trying to make one layer do both is where confectionery packaging usually goes wrong, and it is why so many ranges use a bag-in-box even though it looks like two packs for one product.

Where a range is sold quickly and locally, the inner can often be dropped, and the carton alone is enough. Where stock sits through a season or ships internationally, the inner earns its cost several times over in product that arrives sellable.

Counts, weights and what the label has to say

Confectionery is usually sold by weight rather than by count, and the declared weight has to be achievable after settling. A box filled to a count that comes in slightly under weight is a labelling problem rather than a packaging one, but it is discovered at the packing bench, so it is worth agreeing the fill method before the boxes are made.

description:
Kraft Candy Favor Boxes, and Sweets That Touch the Board

The most common mistake with a candy favour box is a food safety one rather than a structural one. Decorative boxes are frequently not made to food contact standards, and loose sweets go straight into them anyway. At Kraft Box Pack we ask first whether the sweets touch the Kraft Candy Favor Box directly, because that answer changes the board.

If the contents are individually wrapped, almost any board will do. If they are not, the box is food packaging and has to be specified as such.

Sugar reacts to the room

Hard candy takes on moisture

Boiled sweets are hygroscopic — they pull water from the air and go tacky, then weld together into a single mass. In a permeable box on a humid day that happens within hours, and it is why loose hard candy usually needs a wrapped or lined inner.

Chocolate blooms with heat

Chocolate that warms and re-sets develops a pale surface, and although it is harmless it looks like age. A favour box sitting in a marquee in July is a warm place, and no packaging prevents that — only the timing of when the boxes are filled does.

Oils and colours transfer

Some sweets carry colour that will mark uncoated board, particularly where they have softened. A coated inner face keeps the box looking new even where the contents have not behaved.

Key elements of candy favour box design

  1. Food-grade board wherever sweets touch the box directly.

  2. A liner or wrapped inner for hygroscopic contents.

  3. Board caliper set from the weight, since candy is dense.

  4. Allergen information carried on or in the box.

  5. A closure that a child can open without tearing it.

Candy is heavier than it looks

Sweets are dense, and a small box filled with them weighs far more than a box of the same size filled with almost anything else. A light board that was fine as a sample bulges at the base once loaded, and boxes carried from a table by their lids come apart. The caliper follows the filled weight rather than the footprint, and it is worth weighing a filled sample rather than estimating.

Allergens travel with the box

Sweets given away at an event still carry allergen information obligations in most markets, and a decorative box with nothing printed on it satisfies none of them. The practical answers are a printed panel inside the lid, a small card, or keeping the contents in their original wrappers — and any of the three is easier to arrange before the boxes are ordered than on the morning of the event.

Comparison with Kraft Event Favor Boxes

The two are the same format with different contents, and the contents change the specification. Kraft Event Favor Boxes may hold anything — a candle, seeds, a small keepsake — so the design questions are assembly speed and presentation. Fill the same box with loose sweets and it becomes food packaging, which brings in board grade, moisture, weight and allergen labelling.

Contents Board Liner Closure Notes
Wrapped sweets Standard kraft None Tuck or ribbon Simplest case by far
Loose hard candy Food grade Required Tuck Absorbs moisture and welds
Chocolates Food grade Fitted tray Ribbon Heat is the real risk
Jelly and gummy sweets Food grade Required Tuck Colour transfers to board
Chocolate coated nuts Food grade Required Tuck Heaviest for the volume
Children's party bags Standard kraft None Tuck Opened by small hands

Filled early or filled late

Boxes assembled weeks ahead are fine; boxes filled weeks ahead are not. Sweets left in a favour box for a fortnight will have taken on moisture, softened or bloomed depending on what they are and where they were stored. The practical order is to make the boxes up in advance and fill them in the last day or two, which also avoids anybody carrying a hundred loaded boxes to a venue.

Small hands and closures

Where these go to children, the closure has to open without a grown-up. A tight friction lid or a well-tied ribbon defeats a five-year-old and the box gets torn open, which spills the contents and ends the moment the box was bought for. A simple tuck or a loosely tied ribbon is the better specification even though it looks less finished.

Within a wider gift range

An event usually needs several formats rather than one, and the Custom Gift Boxes collection covers the sizes above a favour. Using one board and one print treatment across them is what makes a table read as designed rather than assembled.

What the sweets are, whether they are wrapped, and the filled weight of one box. The wrapping answer sets the board grade and the weight sets the caliper.

"Cardboard" covers two materials that behave nothing alike. Folding carton is a single sheet of board, thin, smooth and made to be printed and creased.
